title: How would you estimate how much bottled water the UK drinks each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many litres of bottled water does the UK drink each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: The UK drinks roughly 3.4 billion litres of bottled water a year: about 68M people at an average of 50 litres each, or just under a litre a week. The interesting part is that average, because a minority of heavy drinkers buy most of the volume while many people barely buy any. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many litres of bottled water does the UK drink each year?

Clarify scope first. Do you mean water drunk by UK residents, or water sold in the UK (which includes tourists)? Plain still and sparkling water only, or flavoured and "functional" waters too? Do large office water-cooler bottles count? A sensible default:

"I'll estimate plain bottled water, still and sparkling, bought by UK residents in shops, cafés and restaurants, and leave out water coolers and flavoured waters."

The approach: people × litres each, built from segments

This is a consumer product bought individually, so start from people, not households: UK population × average litres per person per year.

The trap is guessing the average in one go. A single number like "40 litres" sounds fine, but you cannot defend it. Splitting people into a few groups by how they behave gives you an average you can explain and test. That is the same weighted average technique you use in profitability and pricing cases.

Step by step

Start with 68M people (the ONS provisional estimate for mid-2025 is 69.5M; any round number near that is fine if you say it). Then split them into three groups:

SegmentShare of peopleLitres a yearContribution
Heavy: carry a bottle daily (commuters, gym-goers)20%180 (about half a litre a day)36 L
Occasional: a bottle a week or so, plus restaurant water40%30 (about 0.6 L a week)12 L
Rare: mostly tap water40%52 L
Weighted average100%50 L

Then the total: 68M × 50 litres = 3.4B litres a year.

Notice what the segments tell you: the heavy fifth of the population drinks 36 of the 50 litres, or 72% of the volume. That is the insight a client would care about.

Sanity check from a second angle

Per person, per day. 50 litres a year is about 0.14 litres a day, or roughly half a glass. Most people drink far more than that in total, mostly from the tap, as well as tea and coffee. So bottled water being a small slice of what people drink fits the UK, where tap water is safe and free.

Against other countries. Bottled water is the default at the table in much of continental Europe. Industry estimates put consumption at around 208 litres per person in Italy and 167 litres in Germany. The UK at about 50 litres is a quarter to a third of that, which matches the cultural difference.

Against industry figures. The beverage consultancy Zenith Global estimated UK bottled water consumption at 3.2B litres in 2016, more than 50 litres a head, and close to 4B litres in 2022 once flavoured and functional waters are included. Our 3.4B for plain water sits sensibly inside that range.

Which assumption matters most?

The heavy segment drives almost everything. If only 10% of people are heavy drinkers and the occasional group grows to 50%, the average falls to 35 litres and the total to 2.4B litres, 30% lower. So the first thing you would want to check with real data is how many people buy bottled water most days.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I get about 3.4 billion litres, around 50 litres per person. Roughly 70% of that comes from the fifth of people who buy water most days, so the estimate is most sensitive to the size of that group. It's a quarter to a third of what Italians or Germans drink, which makes sense given UK tap water habits."

A weak answer says "68M people times maybe 40 litres, so about 2.7 billion" and stops. The arithmetic is fine, but there is no reasoning behind the 40 and no check.

Common mistakes

  • Using one unexplained average. Segment by behaviour so the average can be defended.
  • Mixing bottles and litres. A 500 ml bottle and a 2-litre supermarket bottle are very different. Convert everything to litres before adding.
  • Mixing volume and value. If asked for market value, multiply litres by a price per litre, not a price per bottle, and allow for the fact that single bottles cost several times more per litre than multipacks.
  • Ignoring scope. Tourists, water coolers and flavoured water can each move the answer. Say what you include.

Practise it

1. Sixty per cent of the volume is sold in large supermarket bottles at $0.40 a litre, and 40% as single-serve bottles at $2.50 a litre. What is the market worth?

Show the answer

Average price per litre: 0.6 × $0.40 + 0.4 × $2.50 = $0.24 + $1.00 = $1.24. Market value: 3.4B × $1.24 = about $4.2B. Single-serve bottles are 40% of the litres but about 80% of the value ($1.00 of the $1.24), which is why on-the-go channels matter so much to brands.

2. A client sells only to the heavy segment. How many litres is that segment, and how many 500 ml bottles?

Show the answer

20% × 68M = 13.6M people × 180 litres = about 2.45B litres. At two bottles per litre, that is about 4.9B bottles a year, or roughly 360 bottles per heavy drinker.

3. How would the answer change if the question were "water sold in the UK" rather than "drunk by UK residents"?

Show the answer

Add visitors and remove residents' purchases abroad. The UK gets tens of millions of overseas visits a year, but each lasts only days, so the net effect is small: a few per cent at most. Say that and move on rather than building a full tourism model.

Where to practise next

Try the same segmenting logic on what the UK spends on umbrellas and London coffee sales. For the general method, read how to answer a market sizing question, then drill timed prompts in the market sizing drills.
